assumptions: "canonical" is not formalized anywhere in this work, which is why this is DECLARED and not open to refutation as stated
attrs.evidence: NOT DERIVED, and round 3 did not refute it either. Five natural magnitudes — impure-component count; Σ max(0, |sites(B)| − 1); minimum recolourings; minimum carrier deletions to purify; and the partition-lattice gap |sites| − #components of the site-conflict graph (the minimum number of site merges, and the only one with a matroid meaning) — are pairwise distinct, all ten pairs separated by explicit federations. That shows the theorem FIXES no magnitude; it does not show none is canonical, because "canonical" has not been defined. The research pass filed this as "canonical magnitude REFUTED"; that is a polarity and formalization error and is not adopted. Sharper evidence against all five: the zero set agrees between the binary constraint multigraph and its incidence-graph subdivision while the magnitudes do not — minimum recolouring reads 2 on a three-site triangle and 4 on its subdivision. THE CLASS IS NAMED DELIBERATELY: what is proved is invariance under THAT ONE normalization, not under some unspecified family of carrier transformations, and "carrier-invariant" should not be published as a general phrase until such a class is defined.
attrs.review_focus: A declared index is the kind of thing that gets cited as if it were derived. If a magnitude is wanted, the first job is to say what "canonical" would mean — invariance under which operations? — and the carrier-invariance failure is the sharpest available test.
attrs.statement: The MAGNITUDE of κₛ is a canonical invariant.
